_note: Case files shown after each boss and in the Tower Journal. 'real_world' text must stay factual: each line names its source and year. The 'story' pages are made up, based on what really happens. Plain ASCII only (the pixel font has no accents or curly quotes).

lessons.title: Case file 1: The pork barrel scam

trick.name: Follow the money
trick.text: When the paper says money went to a good cause but you cannot find the cause, someone is taking a cut. Look up where the money was sent. Ask who endorsed it, who picked the group, and who got a share back.

real_world.text: For years each lawmaker had a yearly fund, the PDAF or 'pork barrel', for local projects. A Commission on Audit special audit of 2007 to 2009 flagged billions of pesos sent to NGOs, many of them doubtful. In November 2013 the Supreme Court declared the PDAF unconstitutional.
real_world.sources: Belgica v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 208566 (2013). COA special audit, 2007-2009 PDAF. Inquirer; Rappler.
real_world.more: In 2018 the Sandiganbayan convicted the businesswoman at the center of the scam of plunder, and more convictions followed. A former senator tried in the same case was acquitted of plunder. Cases like this take years, and proving who got what is hard.
real_world.more_sources: Sandiganbayan decisions, Dec. 2018 and 2019 (Inquirer, Philstar, Rappler).

story.text: Aling Nena's barangay was promised a livelihood program from a lawmaker's fund. The NGO that took the money had an address that turned out to be an empty lot. No sewing machines ever came. Millions went to people who never helped her village.

lessons.action: COA audit reports are published. When a group says it helps your community, look it up: does it have an office, members and a record? Ask your barangay and your representative's office in writing where the money went.

words.meaning: The Commission on Audit. It checks how government money is spent.
Priority Development Assistance Fund, the lawmakers' 'pork barrel'. Struck down in 2013.
A secret cut paid to an official for sending money to someone.

lessons.title: Case file 2: Lies that look real

trick.name: Who, when, how
trick.text: A quote can be cut so it says the opposite. A crowd of supporters can be fake accounts. A video can be edited. Before you share, ask: who made this, when, and can I find the full original? Does an independent fact-checker cover it?

real_world.text: Newsrooms and universities started Tsek.ph in 2019 to fact-check claims before elections, following the International Fact-Checking Network's code. Lawmakers have called for probes and held Senate hearings on alleged paid 'troll farms' and fake accounts. Some claims made in those hearings are disputed.
real_world.sources: Tsek.ph / VERA Files, 2019. Inquirer. Asia News Network, report on Senate hearing, April 2025.

story.text: Mark's lola in Bulacan gets a forwarded video saying her neighborhood clinic is 'closed for good'. It is an old clip with new text added. She skips her check-up. Lies spread faster than corrections, and the people who profit from the confusion are not the ones who pay for it.

lessons.action: Pause before you share. Search the claim on tsek.ph or with a fact-checker you trust. Look for the original source, not a screenshot of it. Check the date.

words.meaning: A group paid to post fake or misleading content, often with fake accounts.
An automated account that pretends to be a real person.
Looking for the original source and independent proof of a claim.

lessons.title: Case file 3: Buying votes

trick.name: Name the price
trick.text: A handout before an election is not kindness if it comes with a request for your vote. Ask: who is paying for this, and what will they take back once they are in office?

real_world.text: Vote-buying and vote-selling are election offenses under Section 261 of the Omnibus Election Code (1985), for the giver and the taker. COMELEC has a Committee on Kontra Bigay that takes reports, and its 2025 rules count digital payments such as e-wallets as possible vote-buying.
real_world.sources: Omnibus Election Code (BP 881), Sec. 261. COMELEC Resolution No. 11104 (2025). ABS-CBN News, May 2025.

story.text: Mang Berto takes 500 pesos 'for the barangay fiesta' from a campaign worker. The candidate wins. When the barangay health center asks for money for medicine, the answer is that there is no budget. Five hundred pesos once, against a health center that lacks supplies for years.

lessons.action: Do not sell your vote, and do not accept money that comes with a favor. If you see vote-buying, write down the place, time and people, take a photo only if it is safe, and report it to COMELEC's Kontra Bigay committee. Never confront anyone.

words.meaning: Giving money or gifts to win a vote. A crime for the giver and the taker.
The Commission on Elections. It runs elections and enforces election laws.

lessons.title: Case file 4: Jobs for family

trick.name: Who got the job, and why
trick.text: A government job should go to the person who qualifies, not to the boss's relative. Compare the ranking, the interview and the family tree. A 'ghost employee' is paid for work that is never done, or by a name that does not exist.

real_world.text: The Administrative Code of 1987 forbids appointing relatives of the appointing authority within the third degree, by blood or marriage. The Local Government Code of 1991 extends this to the fourth degree. The Civil Service Commission treats nepotism as a grave offense that can mean dismissal. The Constitution says the State shall prohibit political dynasties 'as may be defined by law'.
real_world.sources: EO 292 (1987), Book V, Sec. 59. RA 7160 (1991), Sec. 79. 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 26. CSC statements.
real_world.more: Researchers at the Ateneo School of Government estimated that about two thirds to three quarters of members of Congress came from political families, in studies covering 2012 to 2019. Counting methods differ between studies.
real_world.more_sources: Ateneo School of Government studies, 2012-2013 and 2019 (Inquirer; research.ateneo.edu).

story.text: Jenny placed first in the exam for a clerk post at the municipal hall. The job went to the mayor's nephew, who ranked far below her. Jenny now works far from home. The town loses a good worker, and everybody learns that connections beat merit.

lessons.action: Hiring and appointments are public. If you think a hiring broke the rules, you can report it to the Civil Service Commission, starting with its Contact Center ng Bayan (text 0908-881-6565). Keep the names, dates and documents.

words.meaning: Giving a job to a relative because of the family tie.
Getting ahead through a powerful patron instead of merit.
Someone on the payroll who does no work, or does not exist.

lessons.title: Case file 5: Flood control ghost projects

trick.name: See it with your own eyes
trick.text: A project on paper is not a project in real life. Check that it exists: the site, the date, the cost and the contractor. Ask who inspected it, who signed, and who owns the company that got the contract.

real_world.text: In July 2025 the President ordered an audit of flood control projects. In August he said 15 contractors had won over 100 billion pesos in flood control contracts since 2022. The public works secretary reported at least 421 of about 8,000 inspected projects were 'ghost projects'. The Independent Commission for Infrastructure was created in September 2025.
real_world.sources: Tribune, 'Timeline: Flood control scandal' (Feb. 2026). Inquirer, 2025. Executive Order No. 94 (2025).
real_world.more: At a Senate hearing in September 2025 a former district engineer testified that he passed 25 percent kickbacks to lawmakers' staff. Those named deny it. In November 2025 the Ombudsman filed the first charges at the Sandiganbayan, over a substandard dike in Oriental Mindoro. Cases continue, and the accused are presumed innocent until a court decides.
real_world.more_sources: Gulf News and Malaya Business Insight on the Senate hearing of 23 Sept. 2025 (the testimony is an allegation). Tribune timeline, Feb. 2026.

story.text: Lola Fe was told a new flood wall protects her street. When the typhoon rains came, the water rose to her stairs again, and she slept at the evacuation center while her grandchildren missed school for two weeks. The wall was paid for. The wall was never built.

lessons.action: Agencies publish project lists. Compare them with what you can see near you. If a project is missing or unfinished, take dated photos and report it to the Commission on Audit, the Department of Public Works and Highways, or the Ombudsman. In September 2025 large rallies across the country demanded accountability.

words.meaning: A project that is paid for but not built, or not built as paid.
The office that investigates public officials and files the cases.
The special court that tries graft and plunder cases against public officials.

lessons.title: Case file 6: Budget insertions and hidden records

trick.name: Ask in writing
trick.text: Secrecy hides everything else. Blacked-out pages, refused requests and shredded records all do one thing: stop you from checking. Ask for the record in writing, keep the reply, and appeal a refusal.

real_world.text: Lawmakers can add items to the national budget while it is being passed. In 2025 senators argued in public over these 'insertions': one senator said the Senate added about 100 billion pesos, and Senate leaders replied that insertions are part of the budget process. The fight is over how much was added and who proposed each item, which citizens often cannot see.
real_world.sources: Inquirer, 'Senators inserted P100B in current budget' (2025). Philstar, Sept. 2025.
real_world.more: The Constitution guarantees the people's right to information on matters of public concern. Executive Order No. 2 (2016) lets people request records of executive branch offices through the eFOI portal at foi.gov.ph. It has exceptions that critics say can restrict access.
real_world.more_sources: 1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 7. Executive Order No. 2 (2016). Philstar, Nov. 2016. foi.gov.ph.

story.text: Reporter Ana files three requests for a city's spending records. Three times she gets the same one-line refusal. Meanwhile the city's contractor opens a new office tower. When records are secret, the only people who can check the numbers are the people who wrote them.

lessons.action: File a request for records at foi.gov.ph and keep the reference number. If it is refused, ask for the reason in writing and appeal. You can also read COA's published audit reports at coa.gov.ph.

words.meaning: Freedom of Information: the right to request government records.
An item added to the national budget while it is being passed.
Blacking out parts of a document before it is shown.

pages.title: The real numbers
pages.body: Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index scores countries from 0 (very corrupt) to 100 (very clean), from experts' views. In 2025 the Philippines scored 32 and ranked 120th of 182 countries, its lowest score since 2012. Behind each number are real people: flooded streets, unfinished roads and services that never arrive.
pages.footer: Source: Transparency International CPI 2025, published Feb. 2026 (BusinessWorld, Philstar).

pages.title: Three cases, three administrations
pages.body:
1. The pork barrel scam (2007-2013): lawmakers' funds sent to doubtful NGOs. Supreme Court ruling 2013, convictions from 2018.
2. Pandemic supplies (2021): a firm with 625,000 pesos in paid-up capital won the biggest contracts. The Senate questioned the prices; COA found lapses but no overpricing.
3. Flood control (2025): hundreds of ghost projects reported. Cases are in court.
pages.footer: Sources: Belgica v. Ochoa (2013); Sandiganbayan, 2018; Philstar and Inquirer, 2021; Tribune timeline, Feb. 2026.

pages.title: What the cases share
pages.body: Public money, doubtful companies, missing proof and secrecy. Each case came to light through audits, reporters, whistleblowers or citizens who checked. People accused are presumed innocent until a court decides. Cases are slow, and some end in acquittal. Corruption is not owned by one party, and the safeguards are the same each time.

pages.title: Four habits
pages.body:
1. Check the source: who, when, how.
2. Follow the money: compare announced budgets with what you can see.
3. Ask in writing: a request leaves a trail.
4. Say no to the small stuff: do not sell your vote, and do not pay a fixer.

pages.title: Where to report
pages.body:
Office of the Ombudsman: complaints against public officials (ombudsman.gov.ph).
Commission on Audit: audit reports (coa.gov.ph).
COMELEC Kontra Bigay: vote-buying.
Civil Service Commission: Contact Center ng Bayan, text 0908-881-6565.
ARTA: red tape and fixers (arta.gov.ph).
pages.footer: Contact details change. Check each official site before you send anything.

pages.title: Filing a complaint takes effort
pages.body: A complaint to the Ombudsman needs a sworn complaint-affidavit and your evidence. There is no filing fee, but a notary charges to swear it. Keep dated photos, documents and names. Your safety comes first: never confront anyone if it is not safe.
pages.footer: Source: Office of the Ombudsman, 'Filing of Complaint' (ombudsman.gov.ph).
